segments.caption: A food app says its average delivery time is 32 minutes.
But it only checked 100 orders. How sure can it be?
A confidence interval answers that.
Here's the definition, in simple words.
A confidence interval is a range of values that likely contains the true average.
Instead of one number, you give a range: 30 to 34 minutes.
And a confidence level, like 95%, tells you how reliable that range is.
Why a range? Because every sample gives a slightly different average.
Check another 100 orders, and you might get 31, or 33.5.
One number alone hides that wobble.
The range is the sample average, plus or minus a margin of error.
First, the standard error: the spread of the data, divided by the square root of the sample size.
Here, the spread is 10 minutes, and the square root of 100 is 10. So the standard error is 1 minute.
For 95%, go about two standard errors each way: 32, plus or minus 2.
Now the tricky part: what does 95% really mean?
It does not mean a 95% chance that the true average is in this one range.
It means: repeat the survey many times, and about 95 out of 100 ranges will catch the true average.
Want a narrower range? Collect more data.
Four times the orders, 400, cuts the margin in half: 32, plus or minus 1.
And with only 25 orders, we use the t-distribution, so the range gets wider: about 28 to 36.
So remember: a confidence interval is a range that likely contains the true value.
Average, plus or minus a margin. More data, narrower range.
Quick quiz!
A survey of 100 people has a margin of error of 4 points.
If you survey 400 people instead, what's the new margin?
2 points!
Four times the data halves the margin, because the square root of four is two.
Next: how do we decide if something is real? Hypothesis testing.
Follow for data science made simple!
